extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent attorneys, law students, and legal practitioners studying patentability (subject-matter) principles
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for deciding whether a principle, method/process, machine, substance, chemical discovery, or foreign invention is a proper subject for a patent under the statute and case law. Emphasises materiality, vendibility, specification disclosure, and public-policy limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: A mere abstract principle cannot be monopolized
rubrics_metrics.description: That a mere abstract principle cannot, under any pretence whatever, be monopolized; the elements of every science are common property — data — upon which every man may exercise his ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A principle is not matter and cannot be sold; patent must be for some new production from those elements and not for the elements themselves. (Cases cited: Boulton and Watt v. Bull, Hornblower v. Boulton, King v. Wheeler, Hill v. Thompson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: A patent must be for a vendible matter / manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must be for a vendible matter — something corporeal and substantial that can be made by man from matters subjected to his art and skill, or at least some new mode of employing practically his art and skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materiality/vendibility is an inherent primary quality of a new manufacture; a thing patentable should be tangible, vendible and capable of being bought or sold. (Statute 21 Jac. I, c.3 discussed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: A mere method, process, or manner of operating is not patentable as such
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere method of making a thing, or a process, or a manner of operating, cannot, in general, be the subject of a patent because it is destitute of materiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law shows substantial doubt whether methods/processes alone are manufactures (Dr. Hartley, Dollond, subsequent authorities). Reasons: lack of corporeal substance, requirement that public should not be obliged to make experiments from specification, and public-policy concerns (monopolies in handicraft trades, apprenticeships).

rubrics_metrics.name: A method reduced to practice by tangible means may be patentable (but really the tangible means is the subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle, method, or process, when connected with corporeal substances and when carried into effect by tangible means, may be the subject of a patent; in such cases the patent is for the tangible means (substance, machine, improvement or combination), not for the abstract method itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If specification describes corporeal and substantial matter, the grant may be valid even though called a 'method'. Watt's case is the leading example: though described as a 'method', the specification disclosed tangible alterations and additions to engines that produced the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a patentee claims a method but the specification describes tangible matter, the grant is valid for that tangible subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patentee claims a 'method' but sets forth in the specification some new substance or machine, the real subject of the grant is that substance, machine, improvement or combination, and the grant is valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically inventors often avoid titling an invention by claiming a 'method' while describing tangible matter; courts will treat the patent as for the corporeal subject described. Nevertheless, to avoid doubt an inventor should take a patent for the improvement/substance itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents for improvements must be limited to the improvement (not claim the whole old machine)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who has an improvement should claim the improvement; claiming the whole old machine as new may render the grant invalid for requiring too much or for covering things already known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several judges criticized Watt's broad drafting; a patent for an addition is good but 'then it must be for the addition only, and not for the old machine too.' If claimed too broadly it may be void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical discoveries: patentable when they produce a new, vendible, beneficial substance or compound
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical discoveries come within 'manufacture' only when they give to the community some substance or compound new and unused, vendible and beneficial — e.g., medicines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is no objection that the properties of the component drugs were known if the grant is for the specified compound. Also, a chemical process that produces a new substance may be treated as a patentable manufacture (cases: Turner v. Winter; King v. Wheeler; Hill v. Thompson; Hill's patent discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: The public are not bound to make experiments; methods requiring experimentation are problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention is not of a thing made, it can only be known by being taught by the inventor or by experiments made on the faith of the description; the public are not bound to make experiments, so a mere process that requires experimentation may not be a proper subject for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a process is fully described, some time and experience may be required before it can be used beneficially by others; because the public need not undertake such experiments, methods lacking material, vendible subject-matter are weak candidates for patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double use of a thing known before not patentable unless subject is a distinct substance
rubrics_metrics.description: A man cannot have a grant for the discovery of a double use of a thing known before; but a patent is not objectionable if its subject is founded on the same principle as another, provided the former is for a substance distinctly different from the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example and citation: Cutler case — if patentee had claimed a new instrument (distinct substance) rather than the principle, the patent might have been supported. Thus novelty in the corporeal article can suffice even if principle is old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign inventions: patentable if 'new in this realm' even if invented abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be granted for a new manufacture which was 'new in this realm' though originally invented abroad; foreign articles when published in this kingdom and having requisite qualities may be patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edgeberry v. Stephens and related authorities permit patenting foreign inventions provided they are not known in the country at the time of application; an Englishman who publishes an invention abroad may still obtain a patent if he applies before it becomes known here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory limitation: new manufacture must not be 'hurtful to trade, nor generally inconvenient'
rubrics_metrics.description: It is enacted that the new manufacture must not be 'hurtful to trade, nor generally inconvenient.' Patents that would monopolize methods of working and thereby be generally inconvenient to masters and apprentices are disfavoured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopolies that prevent skilled workmen or apprentices from using best known methods would be 'generally inconvenient' and contrary to the statute; this public-policy consideration supports excluding bare methods from patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology (mode, manner, method, principle, process) treated as synonymous; specification must describe corporeal subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms mode, manner, method, principle, process, &c. are to be considered as synonymous in patent law, and a patent for a 'method' is only good when the specification describes something of a corporeal and substantial nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary rule from authorities: patents nominally for a method stand only if the specification yields a vendible/tangible manufacture; otherwise the patent is invalid. Courts look past technical words to the real subject described.
